opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core challenge in robotics is that we just don't have internet-scale robot data. You can't scrape the web for examples of robots folding laundry or wiping down a kitchen counter. Every bit of robot data has to be collected, often through teleoperation, and that's expensive and slow. So if you train a robot policy from scratch only on robot data, it ends up knowing a lot about motor control in the specific settings you collected in, but very little about the world more broadly.

Vision-language models have already absorbed an enormous amount of knowledge from images and text on the internet. They know what objects are, what they're called, roughly how they relate to each other, and what it means when someone says "put the dirty dishes in the sink" or "grab the thing that's about to fall off the table." That kind of semantic understanding is really hard to get from robot data alone, but it's exactly what you need for a robot to generalize to new objects, new environments, and new instructions.

So the idea is to start from that pre-trained backbone and then teach it to act. We add the ability to output actions, often continuous, high-frequency motor commands, and train on a diverse mix of robot data. What we've seen is that the model inherits a lot of that broader knowledge. It can follow language instructions it hasn't seen paired with robot data, recognize objects it never manipulated during training, and handle visual variation much more gracefully than a policy trained from scratch.

There are real open questions, though. These models weren't designed for physical reasoning. They don't inherently understand contact, forces, or the precise geometry you need for dexterous manipulation, and you have to be careful that fine-tuning on robot data doesn't wash out the knowledge you were trying to keep in the first place. But as a starting point, it's far better than a blank slate. It lets us spend our limited robot data on learning the physical part of the problem, rather than having to also learn what a cup is.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-trained models inherit internet-learned knowledge, enabling robots to follow instructions unseen in robot data and recognize objects they never manipulated during training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core challenge with robots is data. If you look at what made language models and vision models work, it was essentially the internet, this enormous corpus of text and images that you could train on. Robots don't have that. There's no internet of robot experience. Every piece of robot data has to be collected physically, in the real world, one episode at a time, and that's slow and expensive.

So the question becomes, how do you get around that? And one of the most compelling answers is that you don't start from scratch. A vision-language model has already learned a huge amount about the world from internet data. It knows what a mug is, it knows that a sponge is for cleaning, it knows that if you say "the one on the left" what that refers to. It has a lot of common-sense semantic knowledge and visual understanding baked in.

What a robot actually needs on top of that is comparatively narrow. It needs to learn how to map all of that understanding into motor commands, into actually moving the arm and closing the gripper. And so if you take a pre-trained VLM and fine-tune it on robot data, you're essentially inheriting all of that internet-scale knowledge and only having to learn the physical part from your robot data.

And what we see empirically is that this really matters for generalization. If you train a policy purely on robot data, it tends to be very brittle. It works on the objects it saw, in the scenes it saw, with the phrasings it saw. But when you build on top of a VLM, you'll get behaviors like the robot handling an object it's never physically interacted with, or following an instruction that's phrased in a way it never saw in the robot dataset, or being robust to distractors and lighting changes. That's coming from the pre-training, not from the robot data.

The other thing I'd say is it gives you a very natural interface. Language is how we want to tell robots what to do, and vision is how they perceive the world, so a model that's already fluent in both is just a very good starting point for a general-purpose robot. We're not going to get there by collecting a billion hours of teleoperation. We'll get there by being clever about how we leverage everything that's already been learned from other sources, and VLMs are currently the best vehicle we have for doing that.

r001.rationale: The response says a pre-trained VLM brings internet-learned knowledge to the robot, enabling it to handle objects it has never physically encountered and follow instructions absent from the robot dataset.

astra-6.text:
A big reason is that robots don’t have nearly as much data as we have on the internet. If you train a robot model from scratch, you’re asking it to learn what objects are, how to interpret language, and how to act, all from a relatively small amount of robot experience.

A pre-trained vision-language model gives you a useful starting point. It already has representations of objects and scenes, and it can connect those to language. So the hope is that we can use robot data to teach it how to act, while drawing on that broader knowledge to generalize to objects or instructions it hasn’t encountered during robot training.

The challenge is that recognizing something isn’t the same as knowing how to manipulate it. You still need interaction data to learn the physical part. But you don’t have to learn everything from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-trained models draw on broader knowledge from internet-scale data and can help robots generalize to objects or instructions absent from their robot training data.

sol-6.1.text:
A robot typically has much less training data than a language model or a vision-language model. So if we train everything from scratch using only robot experience, we’re asking it to learn both what the world looks like and how to act in it from a relatively small amount of data.

Pre-trained vision-language models give us a useful starting point. They’ve already learned representations of objects, scenes, and language from lots of images and text. That can help a robot interpret an instruction or recognize an object it hasn’t encountered in its own training data.

The missing piece is connecting that understanding to action. Recognizing a cup doesn’t necessarily tell you how to grasp it, how much force to apply, or what to do if it slips. We still need robot data to learn those things. But we can build on the visual and semantic knowledge in these models instead of having to learn all of it from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-trained models can help recognize objects absent from a robot’s training data, but it does not identify internet data as the source of the concepts or clearly state that this enables performing tasks requiring them.
